The story masterfully balances the stretching and compression of time to serve its emotional and narrative arcs. 

**Stretching of time** is used effectively during the climax of the story—the shooting. What takes only about "thirty seconds" of story time is stretched across four detailed paragraphs. The narrative slows down to capture the mechanics of the young man walking down the aisle, the sound of the gunshots, the "dense and granular" silence, the expression on the shooter's face, and Barbara's inexplicable impulse to take three steps toward him. This stretching mimics the psychological experience of trauma and shock, where brief moments feel suspended in time, and highlights the central motif of the story (those three steps).

**Compression of time** is used seamlessly at the beginning and the end of the story. In the opening, six years of Rabbi Adler's history with the congregation are compressed into a single paragraph to quickly establish his warmth and importance to the community. Following the climax, the narrative compresses weeks (the birth of the baby, the funeral, the media aftermath) and eventually decades ("Years later, when Ruth was grown...") into the final three paragraphs. This allows the reader to see the long-term psychological resonance of that stretched thirty-second moment without bogging the story down in the mundane details of the intervening years.
